4. Saudi Arabia Expands Oil Storage in Japan to 24 Million Barrels
Macro Markets

Saudi Arabia Expands Oil Storage in Japan to 24 Million Barrels

FxBrokerTrust
2026-11-25 07:56
Summary
Japan's METI and Saudi Arabia announced on 20 November that Japan will buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish its strategic reserves, while offering Saudi Arabia an additional 16 million barrels of storage, tripling its capacity in Japan to about 24 million barrels. Saudi Arabia accounted for 42% of Japan's crude imports in 2025.
Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry ( METI ) and Saudi Arabia issued a joint statement on 20 November announcing an expansion of oil storage cooperation: Japan will purchase up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish its national petroleum reserves, while providing Saudi Arabia with an additional 16 million barrels of storage capacity. Combined with the kingdom's existing 8 million barrels of storage, its capacity in Japan will triple to around 24 million barrels.
Japan is topping up its emergency reserves with Saudi crude and granting Riyadh three times as much storage space within its borders, signalling that this year's Gulf supply disruptions are pushing buyers and sellers towards deeper supply cooperation.

Key Points of the Agreement

* Japan will purchase up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish its strategic petroleum reserves, subject to favourable market conditions and the completion of necessary domestic procedures;
* Saudi Arabia will gain an additional 16 million barrels of storage space in Japan on top of its existing 8 million barrels, bringing the total to around 24 million barrels;
* In 2025, Saudi Arabia accounted for 42% of Japan's crude imports, closely followed by the United Arab Emirates at 41%;
* The Middle East accounts for 93% of Japan's total oil imports;
* The agreement secures supply for Japan while providing a reliable outlet for Saudi exports.

Japan's Heavy Reliance on Gulf Supply

The agreement reflects Japan's heavy dependence on Gulf supply. In 2025, Saudi Arabia was Japan's largest source of crude imports, accounting for 42% of the total. Overall, oil from the Middle East made up 93% of Japan's imports, making the country one of the major consumers most exposed to supply disruptions in the region.
That vulnerability was tested this year, when conflict in the Middle East disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and forced consuming nations to draw on emergency reserves. Replenishing those stockpiles has now become a priority for importers, and long-term supply relationships offer a route to rebuilding reserves with greater certainty.
This is a mutually beneficial arrangement. For Japan, a larger and more durable link with its biggest supplier helps secure access to crude in times of crisis. For Saudi Arabia, storing oil in Japan provides a reliable destination for its exports and positions crude close to a major Asian buyer, enabling faster delivery when supply chains elsewhere come under strain.

Storage Cooperation Model May Spread

Japan's purchase of up to 8 million barrels is modest relative to global crude trade flows, but it adds a measure of certain demand at a time when the market is selling off crude amid oversupply concerns. Restocking by consuming nations that drew down emergency reserves this year could lend support to near-term crude demand.
Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group ( MUFG ) expects this model to be replicated more widely. The bank believes there is room to expand existing storage facilities, and that Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern exporters are likely to gain storage access in more countries, as both producers and consumers seek to guard against a repeat of this year's supply disruptions. Should other importers strike similar arrangements, the trend would cement Middle Eastern exporters' long-term hold over Asian demand. Such deals could also help Gulf exporters lock in demand as shipments recover, against a backdrop of oil prices pressured by expectations of oversupply.
(Source: Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, Joint Statement on Energy Security Cooperation between Japan and Saudi Arabia , published: 2026-11-20.)

South Korea & the Strait of Hormuz.

South Korea's exposure is structural in a different way from Japan's. Korea is not just a buyer of Gulf crude; it is the world's largest exporter of refined products from that crude, with Ulsan and Yeosu functioning as the regional clearing houses for diesel, jet, and naphtha. A Hormuz disruption hits both the import side (72% of crude) and the export franchise downstream. The country has hedged faster than most: US shale crude is now a material minority share, long-term LNG contracts span three continents, and government and private stocks together cover ~200 days. The Korean Navy's Cheonghae unit operates in the Gulf of Aden, but force-projection inside the strait remains a US-led function. Korea's refining margins are the best real-time indicator of stress on the entire East Asian supply chain.

Key facts
* · Fourth-largest crude importer globally; world's third-largest LNG importer.
* · About 72% of crude imports transit Hormuz; the US share has grown post-2018 but remains a minority.
* · Government and private stocks together cover about 200 days of net imports. The government's own stockpile was about 97 million barrels before the 22.46 million release announced in March 2026.
* · A single chokepoint feeds the world's largest refining cluster at Ulsan and Yeosu.
* · Naval forces participate in the IMSC and Northwood-style coalitions but rely on US Fifth Fleet for area control.
Vulnerabilities
* · Refining concentration: a Hormuz disruption immediately threatens diesel and jet exports to neighbouring Asia.
* · Petrochemical exports, a top revenue line, depend on stable Gulf naphtha feedstock.
* · No domestic crude; effectively zero pipeline alternatives.
* · Korean shipowners operate the largest VLCC fleet, exposing the country to insurance-multiple shocks.
Mitigations
* · Diversification into US shale crude has been deliberate and ongoing since 2018.
* · Long-term LNG contracts with the US, Oman, and Australia.
* · Co-investment in Petroline-adjacent infrastructure with Saudi Aramco (Ulsan storage).
* · Active member of the IMSC; Cheonghae Anti-Piracy Unit deployed to the region.
Historical context
Korea responded to the 1979 oil shock by accelerating refining capacity for export and locking in long-term contracts with Gulf producers. That export-led refining model is now the country's principal exposure: a Hormuz closure does not just curtail imports, it freezes the export-oriented downstream that funds them.

Inside vs outside the strait: why the Hormuz bypass pipelines matter

Oil & LNG →
Every port on the Persian Gulf coast, from Kuwait's Mina al Ahmadi to Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura and Qatar's Ras Laffan, reaches the open sea only through the Strait of Hormuz, 21 nautical miles (39 km) wide at its narrowest. About 20.9 million barrels of oil a day crossed it in the first half of 2025 ( EIA, 3 Mar 2026 ). Ports on the far side can load ships without crossing it: Fujairah and Khor Fakkan on the UAE's east coast, Sohar and Duqm in Oman, Chabahar in Iran and Yanbu on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast.
Two pipelines link Gulf oil fields to those outside ports.

About the port data

* Source. Port figures come from IMF PortWatch , which estimates port activity from satellite AIS ship-position data. They are estimates, not customs or port-authority statistics.

* Exports and imports are PortWatch's estimates of cargo loaded and unloaded, in metric tonnes.
* Lag. PortWatch publishes with a lag of several days, so the newest figures here run to 20 November 2026. We show the latest date for every port.
* Before and now. "Before" is the daily average from 28 February 2025 to 27 February 2026, the year before the crisis began on 28 February 2026. "Now" is the average over the last 30 days of data for each port.
* Dark ships. Ships that switch off AIS are not counted, so falls at some terminals partly reflect ships running dark rather than cargo not moving.

Taiwan's army reopens its NT$24.7m tender for night-vision and tethered drones after the first round stalled

The army posted a fresh tender on 24 November, seven months after the first, for drones that can watch over troops at night and stay aloft for hours on a cable.
T
TaiwanDefence
Taipei · 25 Nov 2026, 02:57 TST
2 min read
X Facebook LinkedIn LINE
A grey four-armed multirotor drone on a camouflage-covered table in a hall, with a soldier in camouflage in the foreground and President Lai in a dark suit standing among officials behind it File photo: A soldier shows a multirotor drone to President Lai Ching-te during his visit to the army's Unmanned Systems Training Command in Tainan on 11 September 2026. Photo: Office of the President (Taiwan), CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) Liu Shu-fu, Office of the President, Republic of China (Taiwan) commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:09.11_%E7%B8%BD%E7%B5%B1%E5%8B%97%E5%8B%89%E9%99%B8%E8%BB%8D%E7%84%A1%E4%BA%BA%E7%B3%BB%E7%B5%B1%E8%A8%93%E7%B7%B4%E6%8C%87%E6%8F%AE%E9%83%A8_-_55521185151.jpg
TAIPEI —
Taiwan's army has put a NT$24.68 million purchase of night-vision and tethered multirotor drones back out to tender, according to a notice posted on the government's e-procurement system on 24 November. Bids close on 8 December and will be opened that afternoon in Taipei.
The notice, issued for the Army Command Headquarters by its logistics command's procurement office, keeps the case number and budget of a first tender published on 16 April. That round, with bids due on 5 May, never reached a contract: a notice dated 20 November said the army would not open or award it because the tender documents had been changed or supplemented, and that it would restart the purchase under the same case number.
Bidders must post a NT$740,000 bid bond and can download the tender papers online, but bids have to be delivered by post or by hand to the logistics command's tender room in Taipei's Nangang district rather than filed electronically, the notice says. The army set 27 November as the deadline for suppliers to raise questions about the documents.

Fixed price, no Chinese parts

The army will pick a supplier through a most-advantageous-tender process, and the winner must deliver within 180 days of the day after the contract is signed, with Tainan named as the place of delivery, the notice shows. The Liberty Times reported that the price is fixed and will not be scored.
According to the paper, the tender rules out drones made in China and parts or raw materials sourced from China, and a local company offering a foreign product must attach the import declaration. The notice does not say how many drones the army wants, nor does it give camera specifications, tether height or flight time, the Liberty Times said.

Watching for hours on a cable

A tethered drone draws power through a cable from equipment on the ground, so it is not limited by battery life the way a normal multirotor drone is, and some systems also pass video and data down the line. That suits long watches over a fixed spot, such as guarding a camp, while night-vision drones carry low-light or infrared thermal cameras to help ground units see in the dark, the Liberty Times said.
The money was set aside in the army's 2026 budget to test whether the drones are worth buying. The Liberty Times reported in August 2025 that the budget plan listed NT$24.675 million for an evaluation of night-vision and tethered drones and a further NT$6.147 million for fibre-optic drones, which are controlled through an optical fibre and so are not affected by electronic jamming.
The paper added that in November 2025 the army asked suppliers to offer 70 training drones and four tethered power modules, which had to have satellite positioning, hovering and automatic return or slow descent, and no Chinese-made parts. It said the army has not explained whether that earlier buy is linked to the new tender.

Taiwan's Navy Tenders NT$36 Billion for 280 VTOL Drones

Bids close 15 December. The notice names no aircraft, but the Navy's budget plan was reported in August as 280 Shield AI V-BATs.
Delfim de Almeida Nov 24, 2026 | 3 min read
Illustration of a generic tail-sitting drone with a ducted fan standing upright on the flight deck of a grey patrol ship, beside a rugged control case
Illustration
Spotted Nov 24, 2026 by FlightBrief's archive , which watches Taiwan's government procurement system, read by FlightBrief's tenders script.
Taiwan’s defence ministry has opened a NT$35.97 billion tender for vertical take-off drones for its navy, about US$1.1 billion. The notice went up on the government procurement system on 16 November, and bids close on 15 December.
It is the largest call on FlightBrief’s list of open drone tenders by some distance. The ministry’s procurement office runs it on behalf of Navy Command and lists the item only as “smart vertical take-off and landing drones”. It names no aircraft and no maker.

What the money buys

The numbers behind the budget sit in the defence ministry’s spending plan for 2027, sent to the Legislative Yuan on 31 August. As reported by the Liberty Times, the programme runs from 2026 to 2029 and costs NT$36.0 billion in all.
It buys 280 drones, 140 control systems and 82 transport vehicles. The navy plans 40 drones this year and 110 in 2027, with NT$13.77 billion set aside for 2027 alone. The last 130 follow in 2028 and 2029.
The plan gives the reason in plain terms. If China ’s opening strikes knock out Taiwan’s command and communications, the navy wants drones that keep watching the sea and resist GPS jamming. They go to its surface combat groups and its littoral forces.

One aircraft in the frame

The tender is open to any qualified firm. When the budget went to the legislature in August, though, United Daily News described the 280 drones as V-BATs, the tail-sitting drone made by the American company Shield AI . The Liberty Times noted that outside attention had focused on the V-BAT, and that the notice does not specify one.
Shield AI already flies in Taiwan. On 13 October it said it had delivered the coast guard’s first V-BAT with Taiwan’s AIDC, under a contract won in July.
The rules favour a maker with a track record. Bidders must prove they have already built or supplied similar equipment, with acceptance records or invoices; a contract alone does not count. Each puts up a NT$50 million bond.
The ministry will choose the most advantageous bid rather than the cheapest, and price counts for at least 20% of the score. Only one firm wins. The purchase is marked as touching national security, and it sits outside Taiwan’s commitments under the WTO’s procurement agreement, so no foreign bidder has a treaty right to compete.

Beside the coast guard’s buy

The scale shows next to the coast guard’s own drone programme. Its officials told legislators in April that it would spend about NT$2.1 billion on 451 vertical take-off drones, Taiwanese papers reported. Its tender for the 18 medium-range drones in that plan, worth NT$782.7 million, closes on 25 November.
The navy is also buying a domestic drone in the same budget. United Daily News reported NT$16.79 billion for 32 Albatross II drones from the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, Taiwan’s state weapons laboratory.
The bids for the 280 drones will be opened at the defence ministry in Taipei at 10:00 on 15 December. Unless at least three qualified firms have bid, the ministry will not open them.

Taiwan to acquire, develop drones to strengthen defense, boost exports

November 22, 2026
2 minute read
Taiwan military personnel display a domestically developed drone in Taichung in October 2026. ANADOLU/GETTY IMAGES
FORUM Staff
Taiwan is investing in autonomous systems, including aerial and sea drones, that have been used widely in the Russia-Ukraine and Iran conflicts. Taiwan recently approved a $7.4 billion drone defense bill, and its military wants to acquire more than 1,400 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones, 200,000 attack drones, and 1,320 one-way attack uncrewed surface vessels (USV), the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency reported.
Taiwan officials, defense researchers and international companies highlighted the growing importance of uncrewed maritime systems, super intelligence — also known as artificial intelligence — and domestic defense manufacturing during a sea drone exhibition in Taipei in late October 2026. The event showcased how sea drones can monitor around Taiwan, a self-governed island that the Chinese Communist Party threatens to annex by force.
Taipei is prioritizing developing uncrewed systems technologies for economic and strategic reasons. It seeks to supply trusted uncrewed systems to international partners while strengthening Taiwan’s ability to defend itself.
To become a top drone exporter, Taipei must establish three pillars to a domestic industry, officials said at the Taiwan Drone International Forum: forge supply chains that do not involve China; develop and integrate super intelligence into autonomous platforms such as uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAV) to allow decision-making and navigation even during jamming attempts; and finalize international partnerships to allow joint research and development, technology transfers, and collaborative manufacturing.
Demand is spurring the effort. Taiwan exported about 210,000 drones worth $237.6 million between January and July 2026, already surpassing its 2025 total, the Taipei-based CommonWealth Magazine reported.
Taiwan has the expertise and industrial foundation to manufacture sea drones, analysts say, noting electronics manufacturers, precision-machinery suppliers, and motor producers and manufacturers can produce uncrewed systems. Taiwan also is seeking partners to produce battle-tested systems with enhanced software. For instance, the Taiwan Coast Guard plans to buy 25 USVs from United States-based Maritime Tactical Systems that will be manufactured in Taiwan and the U.S.
“If you’ve got a lot of small USVs out there doing a lot of different missions, it really takes a load off of the Coast Guard and the Navy and what some of their gray hull ships are doing,” company executive Seamus Flatley told AFP.
Sea drones, which can be built faster than a warship or submarine, are a relatively low-cost asset that can complicate an adversary’s plans. Global interest in uncrewed underwater vehicles also has soared since the Middle East conflict began in February 2026.

...

The drone forum coincided with the opening in Taipei of the Global UAV Academy, a nongovernmental agency designed as a hub for training, technical certification and production. Officials said the initiative will connect industry, government, academia and research institutions, making Taiwan’s drone efforts more flexible and integrated.
The academy has signed cooperation and training agreements with the Japan Drone Consortium, Palau Community College, the Polish Chamber of Unmanned Systems, Taiwan’s National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology — a military research and development center — and the U.S.-based Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International.

Procurement seeks to bolster surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Navy is moving ahead with plans to procure 280 intelligent vertical takeoff and landing drones.
The defense ministry’s Department of Procurement issued an open tender on Monday, per Liberty Times.
The procurement has a budget of NT$35.97 billion (US$1.09 billion), and the contract will be awarded to the bidder offering the most advantageous proposal. Bids are scheduled to be opened on Dec. 15, according to Liberty Times.
The four-year project includes 280 drones, 140 control systems, and 82 transport vehicles. It aims to strengthen surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities in the Taiwan Strait and ensure the military can maintain battlefield awareness even under PLA attacks and electronic jamming.
Bidders must provide a NT$50 million bid bond, and at least three qualified companies must submit bids for the tender to proceed, Liberty Times reported.
Although products such as the V-BAT drone developed by US company Shield AI were previously mentioned as potential candidates, the tender does not specify a particular model or manufacturer. Instead, it is open to all qualified bidders.

Why Taiwan's military drone tenders keep failing

Sylvaine Li
Sylvaine Li 
November 4, 2026
Share   
Why Taiwan's military drone tenders keep failing

Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense has penalized counter-drone startup Tron Future NT$140.3 million (about US$4.3 million) for failing to deliver 26 counter-drone systems for Kinmen, Matsu and other bases. That is a forfeited NT$49.4 million performance bond plus NT$90.9 million in late-delivery penalties, according to a ministry report to the legislature covered by the Liberty Times in late October. The Army plans to start the project over.

Most coverage has focused on Tron. The bigger problem is how the military sets prices. In several recent drone tenders, the ministry either asked for more than its budget could buy, or set a budget too low to pay for the non-Chinese parts it requires. The first drives good suppliers away. The second rewards suppliers who cheat. So far, the government's fixes mostly target suppliers, not prices.

The Tron contract

In August 2022, people in Xiamen flew consumer drones over Taiwanese military posts on Kinmen and posted the videos online. The ministry promised a permanent system to detect and jam drones around Kinmen and Matsu. Four years later, troops there are getting handheld jammers instead.
* Date | Event
* Aug 2022 | Chinese civilian drones overfly Kinmen military posts.
* Nov 2023 | First, research-funded contract with Tron terminated after its radar partner did not join.
* Mar 2024 | Control Yuan censures the ministry for funding acquisition as research and approving a partnership on verbal assurances.
* Apr 2024 | Tender issued for 26 systems, budget just under NT$1B.
* Jan 17, 2025 | Tron Future awarded NT$987.81M for 26 fixed-site systems, in the third round of bidding.
* Oct 2025 | First batch fails acceptance testing.
* Mar 2026 | Second failed acceptance test.
* Jul 2026 | Third failed acceptance test. Army asks the ministry to terminate the contract; Koo says the system could not integrate multiple drones on its operating display.
* Aug 27, 2026 | Ministry formally terminates the contract.
* Oct 2026 | Ministry report to the legislature puts penalties at NT$140.3M: the NT$49.4M performance bond plus NT$90.9M in delay penalties. Project starts over.
The ministry says Tron received no money under the second contract. Under the first, Tron got more than NT$22 million from a defense foundation's research fund, by Domino Theory's estimate . Tron says it built and tested the system at a loss, in good faith.

Problem 1: asking for more than the budget can buy

The 2024 tender asked for more than the 2022 one. According to the tender document, as reviewed by Domino Theory, the system had to detect very small drones (a radar cross-section of 0.01 m²) at 6 km instead of 5 km, and jam them at 4 km. The tender's technical specs aren't public; only registered bidders can download them. Foreign industry experts told Domino Theory a drone that small couldn't carry a real explosive. A drone carrying one or two kilograms would look at least three times bigger on radar.
The budget came to about NT$38 million (roughly US$1.2 million) per system. A July 2026 US Congressional Budget Office report, cited by Domino Theory, put a full counter-drone setup for one site at US$74 million, plus US$5 million a year to maintain. The two aren't directly comparable, but the gap is large.
Here is how the tender went:
1. Round one (August 2024) failed under a rule requiring three bidders. Local media reported that only Tron bid. Most companies stayed out. One sales rep said the specs couldn't be met at that price.

...

Problem 2: budgets too low to pay for compliant parts

When the budget is low and the cheapest bid wins, the tender usually doesn't fail. It goes to the lowest bidder, and what happens next varies. A capable supplier may take the loss and deliver anyway. An inexperienced one may find it underpriced the job. And some may cut corners to make the numbers work.
In 2025, Hang Jian Technology won an 8th Army Corps drone contract with a bid of NT$2.95 million. The military had estimated the job at more than NT$4 million. Prosecutors say the company's head and a technical director at Real Plus Technology built the drones with Chinese chips and flight controllers, removed the labels, and submitted fake certificates of origin.

...

That makes compliant drones more expensive to build. If the cheapest bid wins, a company that breaks the rules has an advantage until it gets caught. A Liberty Times commentary warned that this lets cheaters win contracts and pushes honest companies out.
Opposition legislator Ma Wen-chun says checking where a drone was assembled isn't enough. Inspectors need to trace chips, flight controllers, radios and storage back to the companies that made them. Otherwise, relabeled parts, or parts shipped through other countries, will get through. Our component risk map covers which parts are hardest to source outside China.

What the government is changing, and the counterarguments

The ministry's fixes so far focus on suppliers. It told the Legislative Yuan that bidders will have to agree to checks on their funding and staff. Companies that fail inspection or acceptance testing will be publicly listed and banned from future bids, including as subcontractors.

...

What this means for suppliers and buyers

Taiwanese suppliers: Domestic military demand looks big on paper, but it's currently unreliable. Tenders fail, budgets get cut, and price caps can make it impossible to follow the rules and still make money. In May, the legislature cut domestic drones from the special defense budget . Since then, the legislature has passed a NT$240 billion drone act, and the Cabinet has proposed a NT$55.9 billion supplementary budget for coastal attack drones. More money doesn't fix tenders that ask for more than they pay for. Meanwhile, export demand has kept growing . Smaller suppliers shouldn't rely on domestic military contracts alone.

...

Taiwan now has more money for drones than it did a year ago. The Tron case shows money alone isn't enough. When a tender's price doesn't match what it asks for, the strongest suppliers stay out and the risk lands on whoever is left. Until budgets are set from what the market charges, not an estimate made years earlier, Taiwan will keep losing years to contracts that fall through, and its best suppliers will keep looking to export markets instead.

Inside the Drone Interceptor Rush Nobody Is Talking About

Friday, November 20, 2026 By Dylan King news 10 min read
Inside the Drone Interceptor Rush Nobody Is Talking About
The U.S. Army ordered more FD-1 drone interceptors from Mountain Horse Solutions in October 2026 after an initial spring buy, rushing a compact first-person-view (FPV) counter-drone system into European testing before basic questions of cost, scale, and pilot supply were settled.
Press releases love a neat story. A cheaper interceptor arrives, troops test it on a Baltic coast range, and air defense suddenly looks affordable again.
Real defense procurement rarely works that cleanly.
When air defense soldiers with the 5th Battalion, 4th Air Defense Artillery Regiment took the FD-1 drone interceptor to Poland’s Ustka Training Area in early November 2026 under Operation Audacious Fury, they were not celebrating a solved problem. They were trying to figure out how to keep a cheap drone from turning into a training bottleneck, a logistics headache, or an expensive disappointment once massed enemy UAVs start arriving.

The Cost Curve Problem Nobody Can Dodge

Nobody in air defense needs a lecture on why firing million-dollar missiles at cheap drones is a losing game. Look at the math. If an attacker sends dozens or hundreds of Group 1 through Group 3 unmanned aircraft—ranging from small quadcopters to larger fixed-wing platforms—and a defender answers with exquisite surface-to-air missiles, the defender bleeds money even when every single shot connects.
Senior Army leaders have said the quiet part out loud. Then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll highlighted that cost imbalance in May 2026, and Assistant Secretary of the Army Brent Ingraham echoed the warning at a Pentagon briefing, arguing the service has to stop relying on Patriot missiles to swat down inexpensive drones. Lt. Col. John Verwiel, whose battalion ran the Poland trials, framed the FD-1 drone interceptor around staying on the right side of that cost curve so high-end munitions stay in reserve for targets that actually require them.
That argument makes sense on paper. In practice, cost per shot is only half the equation.
Cost per effective engagement is the real metric. A cheap interceptor that misses half its targets, gets jammed in contested spectrum, or takes three sorties to bring down one hostile drone looks a lot less cheap once you count the airframes consumed and the time lost. Neither the Army nor Mountain Horse Solutions, a subsidiary of Global Ordnance, has publicly disclosed how many FD-1 units were ordered, what the contracts cost, how many interceptors were expended in Poland, or how many targets were actually hit.
Without those numbers, calling the FD-1 drone interceptor a silver bullet is premature. It is an hypothesis under live stress.

How the FD-1 Actually Works

Strip away the buzzwords and the FD-1 is a fast, compact FPV quadcopter built to chase down aerial and ground threats rather than loiter like a reconnaissance drone. According to manufacturer disclosures and defense reporting from the Ustka trials, it can be readied and launched in under two minutes.
Speed is its main calling card. The FD-1 can exceed 265 km/h in its terminal attack phase, with testing reported around 314 km/h. Range depends heavily on configuration—roughly six kilometers in a basic FPV setup, stretching past 20 kilometers with an external antenna.

Guidance blends human control with targeted automation.

...

Speed of Buying vs. Speed of Sustainment

One detail from the October 2026 order deserves close scrutiny because it points to a broader shift in how the Pentagon buys gear. Mountain Horse Solutions noted that soldiers evaluated the FD-1, flagged needed improvements, and the company turned updates around in weeks—using a rapid acquisition pathway ( G-TEAD ) without waiting years for a traditional requirements cycle.
Three years ago, that kind of loop between field feedback, software or hardware tweaks, and a follow-on order would have crawled through committees. Getting from initial spring 2026 buy to field assessment to a second order in October 2026 shows real momentum.
* Dimension | Traditional Missile Interceptor | FD-1 FPV Interceptor | Practical Trade-Off
* Per-Shot Cost | High (often millions of dollars) | Lower cost profile, though exact unit price is undisclosed | Cheap interceptors protect budgets against massed drones, provided hit rates stay high.
* Engagement Speed & Reach | Long range and high speed for high-value threats | Fast terminal dash (265+ km/h); ~6 km basic or 20+ km with external antenna | Strong for short-to-medium tactical defense; limited against distant or high-altitude targets.
* Operator & Training Load | Crew-served air defense fire control | Requires FPV pilot skill, sensor cueing, and formal certification | Fast hardware iteration means little if pilot certification lags behind deliveries.

...

What Poland Really Tested

Watching the FD-1 drone interceptor fly over the Baltic coast at Ustka also shows how Central and Eastern Europe have become the proving ground for counter-drone warfare. Poland itself is building out a multi-layered counter-UAS architecture through its SAN air defense program, while U.S. units in Europe have stood up mobile counter-drone teams inspired by lessons from Ukraine.

Look closely at what happens when you pair a low-cost FPV interceptor with a Sgt. Stout Stryker and external radar or sensor cueing. A lone FPV pilot hunting blind in wide-open airspace wastes time and battery.

...

If certification takes weeks of dedicated flight hours per soldier, scaling to thousands of interceptors across Europe and beyond will hit a wall.
Third, can domestic manufacturing and allied supply chains keep unit costs low at wartime volumes? Small drones are cheap when built in boutique batches for tests; keeping prices down when thousands are consumed every month requires industrial discipline that many defense suppliers still struggle to sustain.
Watch what the Army does after its trainers finish certifying units across Europe and Africa. If a third or fourth order follows alongside transparent readiness metrics and standardized training tables, the FD-1 drone interceptor will have earned its place in the air defense stack. If quiet silences follow the headlines, we will know the math on the range looked better than the math at scale.

Quantum WIY Industries, the joint venture between Germany-based Quantum Systems and Ukrainian defence partners, has confirmed the operational interception of a Russian Geran-5 K5-K jet-powered one-way attack drone using its SPYS interceptor during live combat testing in Ukraine. The engagement marks a measurable shift in counter-uncrewed aerial system (C-UAS) doctrine, transitioning defensive operations away from expensive surface-to-air missiles toward high-rate, low-cost drone-on-drone kinetic intercepts.

The Technical Threat Profile of Jet-Powered Loitering Munitions

...

SPYS Architecture and Autonomous Intercept Mechanics

The SPYS platform was engineered specifically to bridge the cost-capability deficit inherent in intercepting high-speed loitering munitions. Designed as a vertically launched, high-speed uncrewed interceptor, SPYS achieves a maximum horizontal velocity of 480 km/h with an operational combat radius of up to 33 kilometers while carrying an explosive kinetic payload.
The interceptor interfaces directly with Quantum Systems’ MOSAIC UXS mission management architecture. The system ingests external radar and acoustic sensor tracks, computes predictive intercept trajectories, and automates early engagement phases. Once launched, onboard optical and electro-optical seeker systems execute terminal tracking and autonomous terminal guidance against high-speed aerial targets, eliminating human latency during the final high-closing-velocity phase of engagement.

Industrial Scaling and Cost-Exchange Realities

Kinetic air defence economics remain the central constraint of modern distributed attrition warfare. Firing six-figure or seven-figure interceptor missiles such as NASAMS-launched AMRAAMs or IRIS-T rounds against massed drone strikes is financially unsustainable over extended operational campaigns. The SPYS interceptor is estimated to cost roughly an order of magnitude less than the jet-powered attack drones it targets, inverting the traditional asymmetric cost advantage held by the attacker.
To meet deployment volumes, Quantum WIY Industries has scaled domestic Ukrainian manufacturing capacity from several hundred units per month to thousands of units monthly throughout 2026. The production expansion is supported by bilateral funding, including a procurement package backed by the German federal government to deliver tens of thousands of interceptors for the winter 2026/2027 operational period.

The Defense Department selected seven vendor teams to bring their high-energy laser weapons to Dugway Proving Ground next month to see how well they can blast drones out of the sky.
According to a Pentagon press release issued Monday, the companies and systems tapped to participate in the phase 2 directed energy “shoot-off” against live targets include Allen Control Systems’ Bullfrog HEL, Aurelius Systems’ Archimedes, AeroVironment subsidiary BlueHalo’s LOCUST X1, Kord Technologies’ FIREFLY, Lockheed Martin partner IPG Photonics’ Crossbow, Thor Dynamics’ Laser Armor, and Yrikka’s TALOS drone-based HEL.

Two Tankers Hit Iranian Mines in Strait of Hormuz

Summary

Iranian media report two additional oil tankers struck Iranian naval mines in the southern and eastern Strait of Hormuz while transiting on “unauthorised routes.” This compounds earlier reported incidents and elevates the perceived risk of deliberate mine warfare in the chokepoint, implying a higher risk premium for seaborne crude and product flows through the Gulf.

The latest reports from Iranian media indicate that two more oil tankers have struck Iranian naval mines in the southern and eastern sections of the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of this morning. The vessels were reportedly travelling on “unauthorised routes,” which Tehran will frame as a rules-enforcement issue, but market participants will read more broadly as evidence that live mines are now an operational hazard in multiple zones of the strait.
Roughly 17–20 million b/d of crude and condensate, plus large volumes of refined products and NGLs, transit the Strait of Hormuz. Even without a full closure, credible evidence of active mines in more than one part of the chokepoint forces shipowners, P&I clubs, and charterers to reassess routing, speed, and insurance coverage. Immediate physical supply is not yet clearly curtailed, but effective capacity can be impaired if traffic slows, certain lanes are avoided, or more vessels sit idle pending risk assessments or naval escort.

Historical analogues include the 2019 tanker incidents and the 1980s “Tanker War,” both of which generated several-dollar risk premia in Brent despite limited physical loss. If further incidents occur or if Western or GCC navies formally declare mine-clearance operations, the risk premium could expand and persist for weeks to months. If today’s reports remain isolated and are followed by visible de-escalation and safe-passage assurances, the price impact may be partly retraced, but the market will likely retain a structural risk discount on Hormuz transits for some time.

By maritimescrimes

Footage of the supertanker struck "Tara Gas" the 17 of November in Hormuz. Sources: local social media user on Facebook.
Footage of the supertanker “Tara Gas” struck the 17 of November in Hormuz. Sources: local social media user on Facebook.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards declared two supertankers carrying more than four million barrels had hit mines. The UKMTO and JMIC records for the same week list unknown projectiles, and in fact no sea mine strike has been confirmed.
On Thursday morning the IRGC Navy announced that two supertankers carrying more than four million barrels had struck mines on an ‘unauthorised route’ and were still burning off the southern coast of the strait, Al-Monitor reports . The IRGC gave no ship name, flag or owner, and Al-Monitor could not verify the claim. The New Region reported that the Iranian army added a third tanker hours later, east of the ‘restricted zone’, and said its navigation systems had been switched off.
IRGC declaration on the supertanker struck by the mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Nov. 19. IRNA News Agency. IRGC declaration on the supertanker struck by the mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Nov. 19. IRNA News Agency.

Inconsistence : two versions of the same week

The JMIC log, reported by Gulf News , lists ‘unknown projectiles’ for the strikes that Tehran attributes to naval mines, while the CENTCOM declared that the route has been cleared by the US force and remain so.
Between 13 and 18 November, UKMTO and the JMIC recorded attacks on four tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz: the Tara Gas, the Navig8 Messi, the Dar Salwa and one unnamed vessel. Each is logged as struck by an unknown projectile, and none as struck by a mine. Tehran has claimed mine strikes on four tankers on 16 November, three on 17 November, three on 18 November and two on 19 November, without naming any of them. The only confirmed mine attack of this war, according to the Telegraph , involved limpet mines placed on the tanker Louise 1 on 29 October.

Iran narrative framing

The geography of the Strait of Hormuz complicates claims of a widespread minefield. Moored mines, anchored below the surface, and bottom mines, resting on the seabed, have different deployment constraints depending on water depth, currents and seabed conditions. Drifting mines present a separate, less predictable danger. Yet a substantial minefield across active shipping lanes would create a persistent navigational hazard, making continued commercial transits particularly concerning. The absence of independently confirmed mine detections, combined with ongoing vessel movements, makes claims of extensive mining difficult to substantiate.
Beyond the military threat, Iran’s repeated claims of mine strikes, raise questions about the use of information warfare in the Strait of Hormuz. Announcing attacks on unnamed tankers, without verifiable evidence, can amplify uncertainty and fuel fears among shipping operators, insurers and energy markets.
Such statements may serve a psychological warfare objective: portraying the strait as increasingly dangerous and suggesting that Tehran can disrupt global trade even without establishing a minefield. Whether this is a deliberate coordinated information operation remains unproven, but the potential effect is clear: fear of an attack can disrupt commercial shipping even when the threat itself has not been independently confirmed.

International law reminder

Although not factual, Tehran’s account describes mines in an international strait through and the International law leaves little room for that. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees transit passage that cannot be suspended, and in the Corfu Channel case of 1949 the International Court of Justice found that a state cannot close an international strait to neutral shipping. The 1907 Hague Convention prohibits laying contact mines with the sole aim of intercepting commercial shipping and requires every possible precaution for the safety of peaceful shipping. Iran argues that these rules bind only the states that signed them, but the weight of international legal opinion is against that reading.

Clearance capacity

The US retired its last four Bahrain-based minesweepers in September 2025. Its remaining capacity in the Gulf is three littoral combat ships carrying a new clearance package whose effectiveness is unproven. The Telegraph adds that RFA Lyme Bay has been in theater since June with British and French teams and unmanned systems, also new and unproven, and that clearance would have to be carried out within range of Iranian missiles and drones.

Energy transit and conflict resolution path

UKMTO tracking showed single to low double digit daily transits between 15 and 18 November, against about 27 US assisted transits a day and a 2025 baseline of 138, according to Al-Monitor. The Telegraph reports that Abu Dhabi state tankers continue to leave the Gulf, transferring cargo to other ships off Fujairah or Sohar. The JMIC has warned that further attacks are highly likely over the next 24 to 48 hours.
The diplomatic channel could ease the situation ? After the Iron Gate on Iran plan, at Shenzhen, the Trump, Xi and Putin joint statement made no mention of Iran or the Strait of Hormuz. Trump told Xi in their bilateral meeting that both countries have an interest in energy flowing through the strait, Al-Monitor reports. Trump has signalled he will hold off on another major round of strikes until the new year, and Rubio has said economic pressure is achieving the US objective, while US naval deployment remains intense.
Iran’s position is that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has told officials to end the state of ‘neither war nor peace’, and Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf said Hormuz will never return to its pre-war status. Moreover, the escalade might increase collateral damages, Iranian leadership seek to add pressure on USA and its allies, notably mentioning the capability to target US base on the European ground .

China has imposed new export controls on drone components used by Russia to build and operate Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones, a move welcomed by Ukraine.
The restrictions took effect on Wednesday, the day President Vladimir Putin arrived in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump.
Under a notice from China’s Commerce Ministry , exporters must obtain licenses to ship certain drone engines, radio modules, speed controllers and electric motors abroad.

Vlasiuk said some critical components used in Russian drones were still outside the scope of the new controls.
The measures come as Russia has grown more reliant on China for technology restricted by Western sanctions.
Bloomberg previously reported that Russia obtained nearly 90% of those critical components and technologies from China, up from 80% a year earlier, citing people familiar with unpublished data.

The Turkish Industry and Technology Ministry launched a call for proposals on humanoid robots for industrial applications, offering a 50% grant with no budget cap to projects that aim to outperform rival robots.

Call targets bipedal industrial robots

The Turkish Industry and Technology Ministry on Monday launched a call for proposals on the development of humanoid robots for industrial applications, aiming to develop homegrown humanoid robots that outperform rivals. The program targets bipedal robots made for manufacturing assembly, logistics and precision machining.
The program aims to curb reliance on imported subcomponents while cultivating a skilled workforce and fostering high-value-added ecosystems in robot-as-a-service, edge computing and physical artificial intelligence. Funding covers the entire process, including design, prototyping, testing, validation and real-world deployment.

Homegrown components prioritized

The program gives priority to the homegrown development of software architecture, sensors, control and motion systems, torque-controlled actuators, harmonic reducers, servo motors and robotic grippers. Autonomous, decision-making modules and navigation software are also on the priority list.

Minimum technical standards

According to the call's minimum technical standards, each AI-powered bipedal robot must stand at least 1.6 meters (5.25 feet) tall and operate for at least four hours amid mixed tasks. It must also be able to carry at least 15 kilograms (33 pounds) per arm and lift at least 35 kg (77 lbs.) with both arms from waist height.

...

Power specifications, grant and applications

On power, the call requires batteries that can be hot-swapped in no more than three minutes without interrupting operations, and a recharging capability from 20% to 80% in 30 minutes or less. It also requires Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) of three to five to reach at least TRL 8 compliance to ensure safety and quality, alongside other strict requirements.

Europe is building drone defenses. But can it make them work together?

European governments are spending billions to protect their skies. Turning those national investments into a coherent defense capability may prove more difficult.
Illustrative image of a soldier retrieving an Anafi USA drone during a live-fire exercise at Novo Selo Training Area, Bulgaria, 7 August 2025. (J Marshall/Tribaleye Images)
By Paula Soler
Paula Soler is a reporter at The Parliament Magazine
25 Nov 2026
@pausoler98
Share this page
   ?subject=Europe+is+building+drone+defenses.+But+can+it+make+them+work+together%3f&body=theparliamentmagazine.eu%2fnews%2farticle%2feurope-is-building-drone-defenses-but-can-it-make-them-work-together 
Europe's skies have become increasingly difficult to defend. Drones have disrupted airports, appeared over military installations and exposed weaknesses in air defenses designed for a different era. At least 144 drone incidents were reported across the European Union between August 2024 and February 2026, according to a report from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In response, Brussels put forward plans for a "drone wall" in 2025. A year later, the rebranded European Drone Defence Initiative , the multilayered system for detecting, neutralizing and striking dronesis due to reach initial capacity by the end of December and become fully operational a year later.
Much of the work is taking place at the national level.

...

Turning innovation into contracts

Europe's drone industry has a familiar defense problem: demand for its products is soaring, but orders are not coming fast enough.
EU countries plan to invest €18.9 billion in drone technologies between 2024 and 2029, according to a leaked report by the European Defence Agency . Yet only a third of planned counter-drone and very short-range air defense programs are expected to be delivered by the end of the decade.
In an industry where technology can become obsolete within months, Europe's lengthy procurement procedures risk leaving armed forces with equipment that is already outdated by the time it enters service.
"Procurement is not materializing at a pace that matches the urgency," said Arthur de Liedekerke, a partner and senior director at political consultancy Rasmussen Global.
The government departments responsible for buying military equipment have not necessarily expanded alongside defense budgets, he said, while decades of working with established manufacturers have made it difficult for smaller, more innovative companies to break into the market.
"We need shorter procurement cycles, operational testing with end users and contracts that allow frequent upgrades," he said.
Some manufacturers are already benefiting from Europe's military spending spree.

...

But governments that develop their drone defenses in isolation risk investing in overlapping technologies, deploying systems that cannot exchange data and creating legal uncertainty over when and by whom drones can be intercepted, defense experts say.
“To ensure coherence and interoperability, especially at the data-exchange level, more coordination needs to happen now,” Ulrike Franke, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, a pan-European think tank, wrote in an August analysis .
There is also the question of how much Europe can afford to spend defending its skies.

candidates.source_name: Europe should fund Ukraine’s defence industry as a partner, not a supplier | Chatham House – International Affairs Think Tank
candidates.snippet:
The binding constraints are instead access to capital, production capacity, industrial facilities that are vulnerable to Russian attacks, and the availability of specialist components, particularly advanced electronics and seekers.
Of these, finance is the most immediate concern. The head of Ukraine’s Council of Defence Industry has said that manufacturers are operating at around 40 per cent of their potential capacity because the government is not placing enough orders. That suggests that additional funding could quickly unlock production potential.
However, Europe’s requirements go beyond volume. Advanced air defence, particularly against ballistic missiles, depends on complex radar and sensor networks, high-end interceptors and industrial supply chains that require substantial investment and sustained development. Ukraine’s experience can inform European capability development. But it does not remove the need for Europe to build and maintain such capabilities itself.

The limits of a supplier relationship

There are other limitations on purchasing from Ukraine. Kyiv’s export framework is designed to protect its own forces. Companies may export only if they can also fulfil Ukrainian government contracts. Exports carry no intellectual property rights. And re-export requires Kyiv’s approval and attracts a 20 per cent tax.
Even the drones built at the first Ukrainian joint venture in Germany are currently allocated to Ukraine’s armed forces. These are rational choices for a country fighting for its survival. But they mean that in a crisis, European governments could not assume Ukrainian output would be available for their own requirements, at least until Kyiv’s rules adapted.

...

The European Commission’s proposed €45 billion loan to Ukraine for 2027, the second half of the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, including €31.7 billion for defence, provides an opportunity to shape cooperation. The allocation of these funds will have long-term consequences beyond Ukraine’s immediate military requirements.
Funding can support Ukrainian production for domestic use, establish joint ventures on European territory, or, where EU rules allow a derogation, finance procurement from established suppliers outside Europe, including the United States.
Buying Ukrainian output sustains Ukraine’s defence. And buying from outside Europe fills immediate gaps. But only joint ventures build enduring capacity across Europe. Ukraine’s immediate needs, particularly for air defence this winter, must remain central to European assistance. But joint ventures are where support and European industrial development can converge, and where a meaningful share of the package should be directed.
Partnership offers the rest of Europe a way to learn from Ukraine’s experience of rapid development and operational feedback, while reinforcing the need to reform Europe’s procurement systems.
The partnership should rest on a division of labour that draws on what Ukraine’s circumstances have produced. The war has given Ukraine’s defence industry what European nations cannot match during peacetime: urgency, a tolerance for failure, and feedback loops that are measured in days.
Reinforced by Kyiv stripping out procurement, testing and regulatory barriers, Ukraine’s industry benefits from low-cost mass production and rapid iteration under pressure. That has delivered interceptor drones and long-range strike at a pace and cost that European procurement has, to date, struggled to match.
Partnership offers the rest of Europe a way to learn from Ukraine’s experience of rapid development and operational feedback, while reinforcing the need to reform Europe’s procurement systems. Ukraine is already offering foreign firms the chance to test equipment in near-combat conditions alongside frontline units, through its state-backed Brave1 defence-tech cluster, and to pair with Ukrainian manufacturers for co-production. European states should take up that offer as partners rather than customers.
European states and companies, in turn, bring radar and sensor technology, high-end interceptors, sovereign space-based communications, capital, and production sites beyond the reach of Russian missiles.

European Defence Agency says EU ministers endorsed eight cooperation opportunities spanning missiles and strategic enablers

By Martin Chomsky (Defence Industry Europe)
EU | November 23, 2026
European Defence Agency says EU ministers endorsed eight cooperation opportunities spanning missiles and strategic enablers
Photo: European Defence Agency (EDA).
EU defence ministers have endorsed eight opportunities for military cooperation in a review that urges governments to plan capabilities together before taking national procurement decisions. The 2026 Coordinated Annual Review on Defence (CARD), approved on 17 November, identifies opportunities ranging from missiles and unmanned systems to the infrastructure needed to sustain European operations.
The report finds that agreement on defence priorities has not yet translated into a consistently collaborative approach to purchasing equipment. It recommends considering cooperation at the capability planning stage and incorporating it into national programmes and budgets, with projects prepared to draw on EU funding.
Ministers endorsed opportunities to cooperate on a family of cruise missiles, long-range artillery using multiple launch rocket systems and a family of long-range air defence interceptors. They also backed opportunities involving modular, interoperable unmanned ground vehicles and layered counter-drone systems for force protection and critical infrastructure.
The other three opportunities concern space-based early warning, detection and tracking, a European secure defence cloud and a European approach to strategic air mobility. The European Defence Agency (EDA) identifies these as strategic enablers that allow Europe to decide, act and sustain operations autonomously.
“With CARD, we have identified three collaborative opportunities related to strategic enablers,” said EDA Chief Executive André Denk. “From space-based early warning to strategic air mobility, and a secure, federated defence cloud architecture, these strategic enablers are essential to strengthening Europe’s deterrence and defence capabilities.”
Their scale, cost and dependence on shared architectures and networks make cooperation necessary, the report says. It argues that no single country can develop and support them alone, while access cannot be assumed in every future contingency.
CARD calls for further analysis, stronger member-state involvement and dedicated roadmaps for these capabilities. That work should build on EDA’s activities and Priority Capability Areas, in coherence with NATO.
The report makes five recommendations covering earlier cooperation, planning beyond 2030, joint work on strategic enablers, the full process of capability development and faster adoption of innovation. It stresses that buying equipment is only part of delivering forces that can deploy and operate effectively.
Personnel, training, doctrine, logistics, sustainment and interoperability increasingly determine how much defence investment becomes usable capability. Shared training capacity, common information-sharing architectures and integration of sensors with command and control offer opportunities that can be delivered faster than large programmes.
The review also identifies delays between promising technological results and operational use. It attributes those delays to experimentation, requirements and acquisition being managed too sequentially and calls for innovation to reach the field faster.
Immediate readiness requirements must be balanced with investment in medium- and long-term needs beyond 2030. The report warns that underinvestment may become visible only after several planning cycles, when correcting it would take considerable time and money.
More systematic cooperation would give manufacturers clearer and more predictable demand, supporting production at scale and reducing supply-chain dependencies. Delivering that cooperation also requires stronger intergovernmental support for joint acquisition, capability development and research.
EDA’s strengthening process is intended to provide that support and help CARD and Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO) deliver results. EU incentives, including the European Defence Industry Programme, would support those efforts.
At the 17 November EDA Steering Board, ministers also endorsed a joint statement on defence security of supply. They agreed to increase the agency’s budget.
EDA prepared the report in coordination with the European External Action Service and the EU Military Staff. It is the final deliverable of the fourth CARD cycle, covering 2025–2026.

EDA says six EU countries explore joint purchase of CBRN surveillance equipment and services

By Defence Industry Europe (newsroom)
EU | November 21, 2026
EDA says six EU countries explore joint purchase of CBRN surveillance equipment and services
Photo: European Defence Agency (EDA).
Austria, Croatia, Germany, Lithuania, Slovakia and Slovenia are exploring a joint purchase of chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear surveillance equipment and services, the European Defence Agency said. Any procurement would remain subject to national approval procedures.
The six countries signed a declaration of political intent on 17 November 2026 alongside EDA’s Ministerial Steering Board meeting. It opens the way to possible common procurement under the next phase of the CBRN Surveillance as a Service project, with development expected to finish in mid-2027.
EDA’s new Collaborative Defence Procurement Centre, or CDPC, will support the initiative by helping the countries combine requirements and coordinate purchases. Other EU member states will be invited to take part.
“European defence readiness requires more than ambition. It requires delivering concrete capabilities together,” said EDA Chief Executive André Denk.
“Through its new Collaborative Defence Procurement Centre, EDA can help Member States combine their purchasing power, coordinate joint procurement, reduce costs and deliver interoperable solutions. This is how EDA turns European defence cooperation into concrete results,” Denk said.
Austria leads the project, which builds on cooperation launched in 2018 under Permanent Structured Cooperation, or PESCO, with EDA support. National experts, innovators and industry have worked together on technologies intended to improve CBRN reconnaissance and surveillance.
These include sensors that detect hazardous chemical, biological and radiological substances and transmit information about them. Mounted on drones or autonomous ground vehicles, the sensors allow forces to investigate threats while reducing the risk of exposing personnel.
Specially developed software immediately processes the transmitted data and produces a real-time CBRN situational picture to support commanders’ decisions. Some of the technologies were recently tested during the EU Operational Experimentation exercise in Portugal, demonstrating their potential for operational use.
“The countries that acquire the CBRN reconnaissance and surveillance systems under this project can easily cooperate with the systems of other participating countries. Threats can be detected without putting human lives at risk,” said Austrian Defence Minister Klaudia Tanner.

The Takeaway: Arabian Drilling’s SAR 1.5 billion Khafji contract is expected to add to its results from each vessel’s start date, the company said. Its release of 8 November, before the signing, reported record contracted work still to come of SAR 17.6 billion, and the filing does not say how the contract changes that figure. The filing gives no split of value between the vessels and no profit estimate.

Khafji Joint Operations (KJO) has contracted Arabian Drilling to provide and operate two self-propelled offshore service vessels in a SAR 1.5 billion deal, replacing existing contracted service for two vessels.
Arabian Drilling (2381) disclosed the contract to the Saudi Exchange on 22 November. It was published at 05:03 GMT. The filing dates both the award and the signing 19 November, three days earlier, and lists no related parties.

Two vessels, two terms

The contract covers the provision and operation of the two vessels for KJO. They are self-propelled, meaning they move under their own power, and the filing does not say what work they will do. The first is contracted for 10 years and the second for 15. The company expects the first to begin operating in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the second in the fourth quarter of 2028, and it expects the contract to contribute to its results from each start date.
Contract terms by vessel, as disclosed
* Vessel | Term | Expected start
* First | 10 years | Q4 2026
* Second | 15 years | Q4 2028
The filing gives the total value, SAR 1.5 billion, and no value for each vessel.
The filing does not say whether each term runs from the vessel’s start date, from signing or from another date, so end dates cannot be set from it.
Spread evenly over the 25 vessel-years in the two terms, the contract averages SAR 60 million per vessel-year.
That is $16 million at the riyal’s peg of 3.75 to the dollar. The Edge calculated these averages from the filed total. The filing prints no value for each vessel, and unequal rates would change them.
At equal rates, the two vessels would together average SAR 120 million a year once both are running, which the filing expects from the fourth quarter of 2028. The first vessel alone would average SAR 60 million. The release does not say which segment would report the vessels, and they replace existing contracted service, so the value is not all new revenue.

The contract replaces existing vessel service, and the filing’s two texts differ

The English text says the new contract “replaces two existing offshore service vessel contracts”. The Arabic text reads «يحل محل عقد منصتي خدمات بحرية قائمتين», which is one contract covering two existing platforms, and it uses «منصتي» for the new vessels too. The exchange page gives both texts the same date and time, so it does not show which came first.
The Arabic financial-impact line says the contract is expected to contribute to strengthening («تعزيز») the company’s results. Neither text names the counterparty of what is replaced, or gives its value or remaining terms. The filing therefore does not show how much of the contract is additional to what the vessels already earn.

The backlog the company has printed since September

...

It credits two gas awards on land and what it calls the KJO Dorra award covering four offshore rigs. The company’s filings do not use the name Dorra. The match with the 29 September award, on customer and rig count, is The Edge’s reading.
Arabian Drilling contract awards disclosed since 31 August 2026
* Disclosed | Scope | Term | Value as filed
* 31 Aug | SLB, 11 land rigs, gas | 5 years | About SAR 3 billion
* 14 Sep | SLB, 8 land rigs, gas | 5 years | About SAR 2 billion
* 29 Sep | KJO, 4 jack-up rigs | 4 years | About SAR 2 billion
* 22 Nov | KJO, 2 service vessels | 10 and 15 years | SAR 1.5 billion
Jack-up rigs are offshore drilling rigs that stand on the seabed. Values are the filings’ own; the first three are stated as approximate.
Two of these four are not new equipment. The 11 land rigs are the incumbent units under the company’s previous gas contract with SLB, and the 8 are redeployed from the existing fleet.

...

Land gross profit rose from SAR 80.5 million to SAR 96.7 million. The rise is SAR 16.2 million.
On 12 August the company said it had notice to resume its remaining suspended offshore rigs, and that it expected offshore fleet utilization to reach 100% by the end of the third quarter. The release gives no offshore utilization figure.

What the company says next

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise by approximately 8% to 10% on the third quarter, mainly from the start-up of the gas LSTK and KJO Dorra projects it was awarded. LSTK is the label the filings give the SLB gas work.
That range works out to SAR 876 million to SAR 892 million. The release predates the signing of the vessel contract and does not mention it.
It also raised its 2026 capital spending guidance to SAR 750 million to SAR 800 million, to ready rigs for contracted start dates. The earlier guidance was approximately SAR 700 million.

What the filing leaves out

The filing carries no revenue or profit estimate and no day rates. It does not describe the work the vessels do, name the counterparty of what is being replaced, give its value or end dates, or state any backlog figure.
What to watch: The filing expects the first vessel to begin operating in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the second in the fourth quarter of 2028.
Method: the contract’s value, counterparty, terms, start quarters and replacement are from Arabian Drilling’s announcement on the Saudi Exchange on 22 November 2026.
Backlog, results, segment, fleet, guidance and quotation figures are from the company’s nine-month results announcement and earnings release of 8 November 2026 and its announcements of 12 August, 31 August, 14 September and 29 September.
The per-vessel-year averages, the dollar equivalent at the riyal’s peg of SAR 3.75, the per-unit-year values and the fourth-quarter revenue range are The Edge’s calculations.
Sources: Saudi Exchange, Arabian Drilling, The Edge.

Arabian Drilling Secures $399.8M Offshore Vessel Contract With Khafji Joint Operations Founded in 1964, Arabian Drilling provides onshore and offshore oil and gas drilling services in Saudi Arabia. Image by Arabian Drilling
Saudi Arabia's Arabian Drilling has signed a $399.8 million (SAR 1.5 billion) long-term contract with Khafji Joint Operations (KJO) to provide and operate two self-propelled offshore vessels, raising its total order backlog to a record $4.9 billion ( SAR 18.5 billion) , the company announced Sunday.

Arabian Drilling-KJO contract details

* The agreement, which replaces existing contracts for two barges, covers operating periods of 10 and 15 years, marking the longest vessel contract secured by the Tadawul-listed drilling contractor to date.
* Under the agreement, the first vessel will operate for 10 years, with operations expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026. The second vessel will operate under a 15-year contract, with operations scheduled to commence in the fourth quarter of 2028.
* Arabian Drilling said the contract would begin contributing to its financial results as each vessel enters service, providing long-term revenue visibility.
* The agreement also allows the company to maintain its 100% market share with KJO in this service segment.
* In September, Arabian Drilling signed a four-year , $532.5 million (SAR 2 billion) contract with KJO to provide four high-specification offshore jack-up drilling rigs for KJO's offshore drilling operations.

Crucial quote

Fahad Albani, CEO of Arabian Drilling , said the agreement strengthens the company's longstanding relationship with KJO and reflects continued confidence in its operational capabilities. "This long-term contract marks an important milestone for Arabian Drilling and further strengthens our long-standing relationship with KJO," Albani said. He added that the company remains focused on executing its contracts, strengthening customer partnerships, and generating long-term shareholder value.

Key background

Founded in 1964, Arabian Drilling provides onshore and offshore oil and gas drilling services in Saudi Arabia. Its major shareholders include Industrialization & Energy Services Company (TAQA) and global energy technology company SLB.
The company, listed on the Saudi Exchange, serves clients including Saudi Aramco and KJO and operates a fleet of onshore and offshore drilling rigs.
The latest agreement expands Arabian Drilling's contracted revenue base, with the two vessels expected to contribute to earnings over the next decade and beyond.

Arabian Drilling financial performance

Arabian Drilling posted a net profit of $8.4 million in the third quarter of 2026 , reversing a loss of the same amount in the previous quarter, as offshore drilling operations resumed and cost-efficiency measures supported earnings, according to a bourse filing.
The Saudi-listed company reported third-quarter revenue of $216.2 million (SAR 810.7 million), up 6% from $203.9 million (SAR 764.7 million) in the previous quarter, the filing released on the Saudi Exchange showed Sunday. However, revenue declined 2.9% from $222.8 million (SAR 835.4 million) a year earlier, primarily due to lower rig activity.
Despite the quarterly rebound, Arabian Drilling's revenue for the first nine months of 2026 fell 8.1% year-on-year to $639.2 million (SAR 2.397 billion), from $695.7 million (SAR 2.609 billion), due to temporary suspensions of offshore drilling operations and the absence of extended rig-move activities.

Big number

Arabian Drilling expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise by approximately 8% to 10% from the third quarter, supported by higher drilling activity. The company also raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to between $200 million and $213 million (SAR 750 million–SAR 800 million) to accelerate rig preparations and deployment under recently awarded contracts.
